lead: An arc is a gas made electrically conducting by ionisation. It exists because a hot cathode emits electrons, the gas column supplies ions and electrons, and the anode collects them. The arc voltage is the sum of three drops, and its shape on a voltage-current plot decides which power source can hold it steady. This physics sets the source choice for manual, TIG, MIG and submerged arc welding, and it fixes the duty cycle a machine can safely deliver.
prereq: You need: the heat-source idea from Chapter 4.2 and basic circuit ideas (voltage, current, resistance) from the physics course.

sections.h3: The arc is a conducting gas

blocks.text: An arc is a gas that has been made electrically conducting. The gas between the electrode and the work is normally an insulator. The power source keeps a voltage across the gap. The cathode is heated by the arc and by the current; hot enough, it emits electrons by thermionic emission. Those electrons accelerate towards the anode. On the way they collide with gas atoms and knock out more electrons. The gas becomes a plasma: a mixture of positive ions, free electrons and neutral atoms. This ionisation is what lets a few tens of volts drive tens or hundreds of amperes.

The arc has three regions. At the cathode, a thin cathode drop accelerates electrons out of the metal. In the middle, the plasma column carries the current and most of the visible light. At the anode, an anode drop collects electrons into the work. The temperature is a few thousand kelvin near the metal surfaces and much higher in the column. The cathode spot is small and does not sit still; it wanders over the surface. On DC, magnetic forces from the current path can push the arc sideways; this is arc blow.

blocks.where: V_arc is arc voltage in V; V_c is cathode drop in V; V_a is anode drop in V; E is the column voltage gradient in V/mm; L is arc length in mm. V_c and V_a are nearly fixed; E L grows with arc length.

blocks.text: A plasma arc squeezes the column through a small nozzle. The same three drops remain, but the column gradient is higher, so the arc is hotter and stiffer. That is why a plasma arc can cut or weld with a narrow column while a free arc spreads.

Plot arc voltage against current at a fixed arc length; this is the static characteristic. At low current the voltage falls as current rises, because more current means more ionisation and a better conducting column. In the middle range the curve is nearly flat. At high current the voltage rises again, because the column is constricted and the cathode and anode drops increase. The source has its own voltage-current curve. The arc runs where the two curves cross: at that current the source voltage equals the arc voltage.

A drooping source falls steeply as current rises. It behaves as a constant-current source and holds the arc steady when the arc length changes. Manual SMAW and TIG use drooping sources. A flat source holds nearly constant voltage. It is used for MIG and for SAW with a self-adjusting arc. If the arc shortens, the flat source sends more current, the wire burns off faster, and the arc length comes back. A rising source, whose voltage increases with current, is used in some high-current submerged-arc work.

Open-circuit voltage is the voltage before the arc strikes; it is typically 50-90 V. Arc voltage while welding is typically 20-40 V. The heat does not divide equally. More heat lands at the anode; two-thirds of the arc heat is often quoted at the anode. In DCEN the electrode is negative and the work is positive, so the work receives the larger share. In DCEP the electrode is positive, so the electrode receives it.

Power sources convert the supply to a low-voltage, high-current output with a suitable V-I curve. An AC transformer steps down the mains and uses leakage reactance to droop. A DC rectifier adds a diode bridge to a transformer. A motor-generator uses a motor to drive a DC generator; it is heavy and mostly historical. An inverter rectifies the mains, switches it at high frequency, and transforms it with a small core; it is light, efficient and can shape the curve electronically.

blocks.where: I₁ and I₂ are currents in A; D₁ and D₂ are duty cycles as fractions. The relation holds for one machine, because the thermal limit depends on I² times the fraction of time.

blocks.text: Duty cycle is the fraction of a standard 10-minute period for which the machine can run at a stated current without overheating. A 300 A, 60% machine can weld 6 minutes in 10 at 300 A. At a lower current it can run longer; at a higher current it must run for a smaller fraction. The rated current is always quoted at the rated duty cycle, not at 100%.

figure.caption: Voltage against current for a 5 mm arc. A steep drooping source and a flat source each cross the arc curve; the crossing point is the operating point.

spec.aria: A plot with current on the x-axis and voltage on the y-axis. The arc curve falls steeply at low current, flattens near the middle, and rises slightly at high current. A steep drooping source line crosses it near 245 amperes and a flat source line crosses it near 130 amperes.

examples.question: A welding power source is rated 300 A at 60% duty cycle. (a) Find the current it can supply continuously at 100% duty cycle. (b) If the same machine is used at 250 A, find the allowed duty cycle and the welding time in each 10-minute period.
steps: For one machine, the thermal limit gives I₁² D₁ = I₂² D₂, with currents in A and duty cycles as fractions.
The welding time in a 10-minute period is 0.864 × 10 = 8.64 minutes.
examples.answer: At 100% duty cycle the source supplies 232.38 A; at 250 A the allowed duty cycle is 86.4%, that is 8.64 minutes of welding in every 10 minutes.
examples.check:
import math
I1=300
D1=0.60
I2=math.sqrt(I1**2*D1/1.0)
D2=(I1**2*D1)/(250**2)
t=D2*10
print(round(I2,2))
print(round(D2*100,1))
print(round(t,2))

traps: Duty cycle is based on a standard 10-minute period, not a day, not a shift, and not the arc-on time alone.
The rated current is quoted at the rated duty cycle. A 300 A, 60% machine is not a 300 A continuous machine.
Open-circuit voltage (50-90 V) is not arc voltage (20-40 V). Open-circuit voltage is present before the arc strikes.
Drooping means constant current; flat means constant voltage. Do not swap the source curves when matching a process.
More heat lands at the anode. DCEN makes the work the anode, so the work gets the larger share; DCEP makes the electrode the anode, so the electrode gets it.

quiz.q: Define open-circuit voltage and arc voltage.
quiz.a: Open-circuit voltage is the voltage across the source before the arc strikes, typically 50-90 V. Arc voltage is the voltage across the burning arc, typically 20-40 V.

quiz.q: Why does the column part of arc voltage grow with arc length?
quiz.a: The plasma column has a voltage gradient E in V/mm. A longer column means more ionised gas in series, so the column drop E L increases with length L. The cathode and anode drops stay nearly fixed.

quiz.q: A DC arc has cathode drop 10 V, anode drop 8 V, column gradient 1.5 V/mm and arc length 5 mm. Find the arc voltage.
Why does a flat (constant-voltage) source suit MIG welding with a self-adjusting arc?
quiz.a: A flat source holds nearly constant voltage. If the arc shortens, current rises sharply, the wire burns off faster, and the arc length returns. If the arc lengthens, current falls and burn-off slows. This self-adjustment keeps the arc length steady without the welder moving the torch.
Duty cycle is the fraction of a standard 10-minute period for which a power source can run at a stated current without overheating.

quiz.q: A 200 A, 40% duty cycle machine is used at 150 A. Find the allowed duty cycle.
Why does DCEN give more heat to the work than DCEP?
quiz.a: More arc heat lands at the anode. In DCEN the electrode is negative and the work is positive, so the work is the anode and receives the larger share. In DCEP the electrode is positive, so the electrode receives the larger share.

quiz.q: What are the three regions of arc voltage?
quiz.a: The cathode drop at the negative electrode, the plasma column drop along the arc length, and the anode drop at the positive electrode.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern inverter sources switch at tens of kHz, so the transformer shrinks and the controller can shape current in milliseconds. Research uses high-speed cameras and spectroscopy to watch cathode spots and metal transfer. Wire-arc additive manufacturing uses a controlled arc as a 3D printing heat source. Search next: inverter welding source, arc blow, plasma arc welding, wire-arc additive manufacturing.
